newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION-Nepia a jewel in NZ rugby's crown.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-Nepia a jewel in NZ rugby's crown.

text.p: Wellington, Oct 2 - George Nepia is one of the jewels in New Zealand's rugby history, and vies with Colin Meads for the honour of being the most famous All Black, NZPA reports as part of a series on champions in the Sports Hall of Fame.
Nepia was the sturdy 19-year-old Maori boy who played fullback in every match of the famous 1924 Invincibles team's tour of Britain and France.

He had virtually no experience at fullback before that tour, but grew into the position so quickly that even today there are those who bypass the claims of Billy Wallace, Bob Scott and Don Clarke to nominate Nepia as the prince of All Blacks fullbacks.

During the 1920s he was a key figure in Norman McKenzie's record-breaking Hawke's Bay Ranfurly Shield team, and he was still the best fullback in the country in 1930 when he played in four tests against the touring Great Britain side.

Nepia went close to winning selection for the 1935 team to Britain but when he missed out, he turned to rugby league, winning a Kiwis cap in 1937 and enjoying two fruitful years in the paid ranks in England.
With Nepia, there was always a special charm, a magic that drew others to him.
He was too popular and charismatic to be shunned like others who switched to league, and he was readmitted to rugby union by dint of a special war amnesty.
He continued to play after the war and when he eventually retired, he took up refereeing.
Nepia was one of those players about whom legends grew.
He is so famous even today that he was an obvious choice as one of the inaugural inductees into the Sports Hall of Fame.

The basic facts of his story are well enough known. He was born in Wairoa in 1905 and as a boy hopped off the train with his mates at Hastings instead of continuing south to Te Aute College as had been planned.
So he attended Maori Agricultural College where he came under the influence of American Elder Moser.
With his gridiron background, Moser instilled in Nepia the secrets of tackling and torpedo kicking. Both were to become Nepia trademarks.
He made his first-class debut in 1921 when just a lad of 16, and got his break when playing in the Te Mori Rose Bowl match between Southern and Northern Maori in Auckland.
At the insistence of the great Maori identity Ned Parata, he played at fullback instead of his usual position of first five-eighth, and he seldom played anywhere else again.

Although he was a certain selection for the Invincibles team, he knew so little about fullback play that serious consideration was given to playing Mark Nicholls at fullback in the first few tour matches while Nepia learned his trade.
In the end Nepia was given his chance and responded magnificently.
He was 1.75m in height and weighed 82.5kg, and exuded solidity.

His diving at the feet of on-rushing forwards who used to dribble so much in those days, his fantastic punting, his uncompromising and ferocious tackling and his courage made him a rugby sensation in a team of superstars.
He was never a top place-kicker, but he did kick 33 conversions and five penalties during the tour.
There is a famous piece of writing by Denzil Batchelor, a noted cricket and rugby journalist, which sums up the admiration Nepia drew at that time:

"When I hear others debating who will play at fullback for the Kingdom of Heaven versus the Rest, I turn to stone. It is not for me a question of whether Nepia was the best fullback in history. It is a question of which of the others is fit to loosen the laces of his Cotton Oxford boots," Batchelor wrote.
Nepia was always extremely modest about his achievements on that tour.
He said he would have been lost without Nicholls, and he downplayed the importance of his role in the Invincibles' unbeaten record.
"Some of the matches they could have played without a fullback," he once said.
"They were such a brilliant team; a great pack of forwards and a brilliant set of backs."
In 1927, Nepia moved north to try to eke out a living from a rugged piece of farmland outside Gisborne.
Because he was a Maori, he was ineligible for the 1928 tour of South Africa, and after the 1930 season, little more was heard of him for years.

In those times of the Depression, earning a living was a serious business, and survival, rather than rugby, was a priority for Nepia as he cared for his wife Huinga and their children -- George, Kiwi, Oma and Winston.
He returned to serious rugby in 1935 and although he missed the team to Britain, he toured Australia with New Zealand Maori and played superbly.

The next chapter of Nepia's story moves ahead two years. On the day the All Blacks lost the third test, and the series against South Africa in 1937, Nepia helped the Kiwis to an historic rugby league win over Australia.
He continued to play top rugby after the war, making his last first-class appearance in 1950, at the age of 45 years, 158 days -- a New Zealand record.

It also meant he had the longest first-class career in New Zealand rugby history. In that last match, his son George junior also played, a rare situation in which father and son opposed each other in a first-class match.
During a span of 29 years, he played 129 first-class matches (besides his league stint) and scored 396 points. For New Zealand he played 46 matches, including nine tests, and scored 99 points.
After his retirement he became a living legend.
He showed courage again when he led the anti-South Africa tour marches through the 1950s, two decades before public feeling turned strongly that way.
He was always incredibly popular. Nothing was too much trouble for him, and he was always ready to laugh that giggly, high-pitched laugh.
He maintained one of the greatest moments of his life was in 1986 when he was made an honorary life vice-president of the South African Rugby Board.

Another memorable occasion was in 1982 when he returned to Wales and walked on to the St Helen's ground at Swansea 58 years after he'd played there. The crowd stood for him, first in silence, then in wave after wave of applause.
New Zealanders of a younger generation saw why Nepia was so special when he was guest of a This Is Your Life programme in 1986. He died later that year, at the age of 81.
He left behind memories of a friendly, kindly man, and a rugby player fit to take his place in any World 15.
